report:
Rigorous epidemiological evidence demonstrates that having an induced abortion **does not** increase a woman's risk of developing breast cancer. 

The view that abortion causes breast cancer originated from early retrospective case-control studies that relied on patient interviews. Researchers later discovered these studies were distorted by **recall bias**: women diagnosed with breast cancer reported past abortions far more accurately than healthy control subjects, creating a false statistical association.

To eliminate recall bias, researchers conducted prospective cohort studies using medical records recorded before any cancer diagnosis. These studies consistently showed no elevated risk. 

In 2004, a landmark meta-analysis published in *The Lancet* analyzed data from 53 studies across 16 countries, involving over 83,000 women with breast cancer. The researchers found that neither induced nor spontaneous abortions increase breast cancer risk. 

Based on this body of evidence, major global medical organizations—including the National Cancer Institute, the World Health Organization, the American Cancer Society, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists—unanimously conclude that abortion does not increase breast cancer risk.

**Sources:**
- *The Lancet* Meta-Analysis: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext
- *Nature* Report on Epidemiological Consensus: https://www.nature.com/articles/news040322-14
- *The New York Times* Summary of Findings: https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/26/us/study-doesn-t-link-abortion-to-higher-breast-cancer-risk.html
- *The Atlantic* Overview on Research Methodology and Recall Bias: https://www.theatlantic.com/national/2013/12/inside-faulty-science-abortion-breast-cancer-link/355850/
